list-item.p: ABBV-744 monotherapy in pretreated MF yielded a DLT rate of 52% (11/21), most commonly due to thrombocytopenia (n = 7) and anemia (n = 5).
ABBV-744 led to 33% SVR35 at week 24 and 29% TSS50 at week 12; ABBV-744 efficacy was consistent with pan-BET inhibitors, like pelabresib.

abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKi) are standard of care for patients with myelofibrosis (MF) but can be associated with treatment-limiting cytopenias and do not modify underlying disease. Novel treatments targeting other clinically relevant pathways are needed. Inhibitors of bromodomain (BD) and extraterminal domain (BET) proteins are a promising class of drugs that have demonstrated the ability to modulate key pathways involved in inflammation, fibrosis, and apoptosis. ABBV-744 is a novel small molecule that targets the BDII of BET proteins and has previously been shown to be well tolerated when administered daily at doses of 120 and 180 mg to patients with acute myeloid leukemia. We report the outcomes of a multicenter, open-label phase 1b study of ABBV-744 in patients with MF who received ≥1 previous lines of therapy, including a JAKi. The primary objective was safety, including dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs). Secondary end points included a reduction in spleen volume of ≥35% (SVR35), ≥50% reduction in total symptom score (TSS50), objective response rate, and pharmacokinetics. All 21 patients experienced at least 1 treatment-emergent adverse event, and 11 patients experienced a DLT. The most common events leading to DLTs were thrombocytopenia (33%) and anemia (24%). SVR35 was attained in 24% of patients at week 12 and 33% at week 24. TSS50 was reported for 29% of patients at 12 weeks and 19% at week 24. These outcomes are noteworthy in this heavily pretreated population considering the advanced disease state and limited treatment options for this patient population. This trial was registered at www.clinicaltrials.gov as NCT04454658.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Myelofibrosis (MF) is a chronic myeloproliferative neoplasm characterized by uncontrolled inflammation and fibrotic deposition in the extracellular bone marrow space, leading to progressive bone marrow failure.1,2 Clinically, MF often presents with anemia, constitutional symptoms (eg, fatigue, weakness, and bone pain), and extramedullary hematopoiesis, which frequently manifests as splenomegaly, resulting in marked discomfort and significant morbidity.2

Although allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplantation is a curative therapy for MF, only a small subset of patients are eligible for the treatment due to advanced age, comorbidities, and risks associated with transplant-related morbidity and mortality.2,3 Consequently, treatment for most patients with MF is palliative, with the goal of reducing symptoms and improving quality of life. Currently, 4 Janus kinase inhibitors (JAKis), ruxolitinib, fedratinib, momelotinib, and pacritinib, are approved for MF based on their ability to reduce splenomegaly and improve symptoms.4, 5, 6, 7 However, ruxolitinib and fedratinib are associated with moderate to severe drug-induced anemia and thrombocytopenia, which may complicate long-term use. Furthermore, both drugs are associated with a risk of rapid disease progression upon discontinuation, leading to potential hospitalizations.8,9 In part, to address this limitation, momelotinib and pacritinib were approved for MF for subsets of patients with anemia or thrombocytopenia, respectively. However, all 4 approved agents essentially target the same pathway, are not curative, and do not fundamentally address the underlying cause of the disease, leaving a substantial unmet need for novel therapies with alternative mechanisms of action.

Preclinical studies in murine models of MF have identified nuclear factor κB (NF-κB) as a key pathway activated in hematopoietic cells and demonstrated that bromodomain (BD) and extraterminal domain (BET) inhibition attenuates NF-κB signaling, reduces cytokine production, and reverses bone marrow fibrosis.10,11 Combined JAK/BET inhibition in these models produced marked reductions in inflammatory cytokines and disease burden, and reversed bone marrow fibrosis in vivo.10

Early clinical trials with ABBV-075 and ODM-207, which broadly targeted BET proteins in patients with solid tumors, demonstrated some evidence of disease control. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events (TEAEs) were thrombocytopenia, fatigue, and nausea.12,13 Pelabresib (CPI-0610), which is also a pan-BET inhibitor (BETi), demonstrated notable clinical activity in a phase 2 study of patients with refractory or intolerant advanced MF, including spleen volume reduction and improvement in symptom burden as a monotherapy in patients exposed to JAKis, as an “add-on” therapy in combination with ruxolitinib for patients with suboptimal response to JAKis, and in combination for JAKi-naïve patients. Pelabresib has also demonstrated an acceptable safety profile, with grade 3/4 toxicities, primarily reversible thrombocytopenia and anemia, occurring in 12% and 35% of patients, respectively.14 These findings support the potential of pan-BETis as a therapeutic modality for MF but highlight gastrointestinal (GI) toxicities and cytopenias as potential class effects of broad BETis.

ABBV-744 is a novel, selective BETi that, at low doses, preferentially targets the BDII over BDI within the BET family of proteins. This BDII selectivity distinguishes ABBV-744 from pan-BETi–like pelabresib, and is hypothesized to maintain therapeutic efficacy, while reducing class-effect toxicities (ie, thrombocytopenia and GI). In preclinical studies using androgen receptor–positive prostate cancer mouse xenograft models, ABBV-744 at one-sixteenth its maximum tolerated dose (MTD) displayed antitumor activity equivalent to, or better than, pan-BETis ABBV-075, JQ1, and iBET.15 In rats, ABBV-075 at 3 mg/kg led to substantial hematological and GI toxicity, as demonstrated by the 59% reduction in platelets, decreased Alcian blue staining of the mucosa, and loss of goblet cells in the large intestine. Alternatively, a 20% reduction in platelets was observed with ABBV-744 at both 30 mg/kg (10× the 3 mg/kg ABBV-075 dose) and 60 mg/kg (20× the ABBV-075 dose assessed).15

A first-in-human study of ABBV-744 evaluated its safety, tolerability, and pharmacokinetics (PK) in patients with relapsed or refractory (R/R) acute myeloid leukemia (AML).16 Although the MTD and the recommended phase 2 dose for ABBV-744 were not identified, ABBV-744 was well tolerated at doses of 120 and 180 mg administered orally once daily, with dose-dependent GI toxicities (eg, dysgeusia, nausea, anorexia) and potential bone marrow suppression being the primary TEAEs.

Based on these preclinical data and previous results in AML demonstrating that ABBV-744 modulated key cytokines correlating with spleen volume response and symptomatic improvement consistent with JAKis in MF,16 this phase 1b study was undertaken to assess the safety and efficacy of ABBV-744 monotherapy in patients with MF.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Eligible patients were adults aged ≥18 years, with intermediate or high-risk MF as defined by the World Health Organization criteria (intermediate-1 or high-risk per Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System). In addition, patients were required to have evidence of MF-related symptoms, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status score of ≤2, absolute neutrophil count of ≥1.5 109/L, platelets of ≥100 109/L, splenomegaly, and a creatinine clearance value of ≥40 mL/min. Exclusion criteria included concomitant CYP3A inhibitor use and previous exposure to BETis. Further details on the eligibility criteria are provided in the supplemental Methods.

sec.title: Study design and treatment
sec.p: This phase 1b multicenter, open-label study had a planned enrollment of ∼130 patients across 60 sites worldwide and was designed with 4 distinct segments to evaluate ABBV-744. Starting doses of ABBV-744 were informed by the first-in-human study of ABBV-744 in AML.16 Segment A, the focus of this report, investigated ABBV-744 monotherapy in patients with previous exposure to at least 1 JAKi, exploring multiple dose levels and schedules in 21-day cycles: continuous dosing (120 mg daily until unacceptable toxicity or progressive disease) or intermittent dosing (180 mg daily for 14 days followed by a treatment-free interval of 7 days until unacceptable toxicity or progressive disease). Preliminary data from patients with MF treated at these doses determined that the doses were not tolerated and lower doses of ABBV-744 monotherapy were evaluated per dose reduction guidelines. Lower dosing or alternative dose regimens included, but were not limited to, 5 mg continuous, 10 mg continuous, 20 mg continuous, 5 mg intermittent, 10 mg intermittent, 20 mg intermittent, or 40 mg intermittent, based on discussion between the principal investigator and medical monitor. Refer to the supplemental Methods for the full, planned study design, study schematic (supplemental Figure 1), and dose reduction guidelines (supplemental Table 1). This study was registered at ClinicalTrials.gov (identifier: NCT04454658).

The study was conducted in accordance with the International Council for Harmonisation good clinical practice guidelines and the ethical principles that have their origin in the Declaration of Helsinki. The protocol and amendments were approved by the institutional review board and independent ethics committee at each participating site. All patients provided written informed consent.

sec.title: End points and assessments
sec.p: The primary end point of the study was the determination of the AEs (coded per Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 27.0 and graded per National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 5.0) profile of ABBV-744 in patients with MF, including dose-limiting toxicities (DLTs). Secondary end points included the proportion of patients achieving a reduction in spleen volume of ≥35% (SVR35) at weeks 12 and 24, the proportion of patients with a ≥50% reduction in total symptom score (TSS50) at weeks 12 and 24, best objective response rate (ORR) per International Working Group–Myeloproliferative Neoplasms Research and Treatment and European LeukemiaNet consensus response criteria,17 and PK parameters including maximum observed plasma concentration and area under the plasma concentration-time curve.17 Patients continued treatment until progression or unacceptable toxicity, after which a 30-day safety follow-up visit was conducted. After disease progression, posttreatment follow-up visits were conducted every 12 weeks for up to 1 year from cycle 1 day 1 or until study discontinuation, whichever was longer.

sec.title: PK assessments
sec.p: Serial blood samples for PK analysis of ABBV-744 were collected on cycle 1 day 1 and cycle 1 day 8 at before dose, and 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, and 24 hours (on day 1 only) after dose. Plasma concentrations of ABBV-744 were determined using a validated method. PK parameters were estimated using noncompartmental analyses.

sec.title: Biomarker assessments
sec.p: Plasma was collected at baseline (cycle 1 day 1); cycle 1 day 15, cycle 2 day 1, cycle 3 day 1, cycle 4 day 1, and cycle 5 day 1 visits; visits occurring every 4 cycles thereafter (cycle 9 day 1, cycle 13 day 1, etc); and at time of treatment discontinuation, and was analyzed using the 129-analyte Human ExplorerMAP version 1.0 panel. Proteins associated with BDII pharmacodynamic activity (ie, adiponectin and interleukin-18 [IL-18]),18,19 NF-κB signaling (eg, β2-microglobulin [B2M], C-reactive protein, CD40 ligand), and/or constitutional symptom control (eg, tissue inhibitor of metalloproteinase 1 [TIMP-1])20 were assessed, and on-study levels were calculated as a percent change from baseline. To account for dose interruptions and/or dose reductions, average daily dose (total amount of study drug taken divided by number of days in between first and last dose), as opposed to cohort enrolled (120, 80, and 40 mg), was used when assessing changes in protein levels.

sec.title: Statistical analyses
sec.p: All analyses were performed on the full analysis set, which included all patients who received at least 1 dose of study drug. Summary statistics were calculated including number and percentage for categorical variables and number of patients, mean, standard deviation, median, minimum, and maximum for continuous variables. Two-sided 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were provided as appropriate.

Demographics, baseline disease characteristics, and safety data are summarized by descriptive statistics. SVR35 from baseline along with the corresponding 95% CIs were derived by the Clopper-Pearson method; and TSS50, a patient-reported outcome on the MF symptom assessment form version 4.0, was summarized with an exact 95% CI derived by the Clopper-Pearson method. Additional efficacy measures such as ORR (complete remission plus partial remission) and corresponding 95% CI were derived by the Clopper-Pearson method.

sec.title: Patient demographics and disposition
sec.p:
The data cutoff date for this analysis was 30 October 2024; median follow-up was 21.7 months (95% CI, 14.0-24.4). A total of 21 patients were treated with at least 1 dose of ABBV-744; 20 patients received continuous ABBV-744 (120 mg/kg, n = 8; 80 mg/kg, n = 6; 40 mg/kg, n = 6), and 1 patient received intermittent ABBV-744 at 180 mg (14 days). Based on the totality of emerging safety and PK data, recruitment into the 180 mg intermittent cohort was suspended after enrollment of a single patient. The median age of patients was 63 years (range, 42-78) and 57% were male. By the Dynamic International Prognostic Scoring System, 5 patients (24%) had intermediate-1, 15 (71%) had intermediate-2, and 1 (5%) had high-risk disease. The median number of previous lines of systemic therapy was 2 (range, 1-5). Additional baseline demographics and disease characteristics of patients are summarized in Table 1.Table 1.

Dose interruptions occurred in 71% of patients overall; the median number of interruptions was 2 (range, 1-43), with the most interruptions occurring at the 120 mg/kg dose level. Dose reductions occurred in 57% of patients, and two-thirds of these patients required only 1 dose reduction. sec.title: Safety
sec.p:
All 21 patients experienced at least 1 TEAE and 18 (86%) had at least 1 grade 3 to 4 TEAE. The most frequent events were thrombocytopenia (67%), diarrhea (62%), anemia (48%), and nausea (33%). For more details, supplemental Table 2 shows frequency of any grade TEAEs in >15% of patients; supplemental Figures 3 and 4 show platelet and hemoglobin counts over time, respectively. Grade 3 to 4 events occurring in >10% of patients were anemia (48%), thrombocytopenia (38%), and pneumonia (14%). TEAEs leading to DLTs were observed in 11 patients (52%): 4 (50%) in the 120-mg cohort, 3 (50%) in the 80-mg cohort, 3 (50%) in the 40-mg cohort, and 1 (100%) in the 180-mg cohort (Table 4). The most common TEAEs leading to DLTs were thrombocytopenia (33%) and anemia (24%). Three patients in the 40-mg cohort had co-occurring DLTs of thrombocytopenia and anemia. One patient in the 80-mg cohort had >1 DLT occurring separately, hyponatremia and anemia. Three patients experienced TEAEs that led to study drug discontinuation: grade 3 diarrhea and grade 1 vomiting (in 1 patient), and in 1 patient each, grade 3 platelet count decreased and grade 3 transformation to acute AML.Table 4.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p:
The proportion of patients achieving SVR35 was 24% (n = 5; 95% CI, 8.2-47.2) at week 12, 33% (n = 7; 95% CI, 14.6-57.0) at week 24, and 33% (n = 7; 95% CI, 14.6-57.0) at week 36 (Figure 1; Table 5). Overall, TSS50 was observed in 29% of patients (n = 6; 95% CI, 11.3-52.2) by week 12, 19% (n = 4; 95% CI, 5.4-41.9) at week 24, and 14% (n = 3; 95% CI, 3.0-36.3) at week 36 (supplemental Figure 5A-B; Table 5).Figure 1.

Among the entire study population (N = 21), ORR was 5%, with 1 patient achieving partial remission (120-mg cohort, 1/8 patients [13%]). The best overall responses across all patients included clinical improvement in 7 patients (33%) and stable disease in 5 patients (24%). Progressive disease was observed in 1 patient (5%), whereas response data were not available for 7 patients (33%) who discontinued treatment before their first assessment. Although no patient achieved complete remission, no responding patient experienced relapse, and 9 patients (43%) were receiving ongoing treatment as of the data cutoff date (Figure 2). Of 21 patients, 7 had available paired data on postbaseline MF grade; of these, 4 had no change in MF grade, 2 decreased from MF2 to MF0, and 1 decreased from MF3 to MF2.Figure 2.

sec.title: PK
sec.p: ABBV-744 exposures were generally dose proportional (supplemental Table 3). The dose-normalized maximum observed plasma concentration (10.3 ng/mL per mg, 42%) was observed at a median time to peak drug concentration of 2 hours (range, 1-6); the dose-normalized area under the plasma concentration-time curve was 69.1 ng·h/mL per mg (52%).

sec.title: Biomarker analysis
sec.p: Thirteen patients had both baseline and on-study plasma samples assessed. Of these 13 patients, 4 patients had an average ABBV-744 daily dose of 19 mg (18, 18, 18, and 22 mg daily, respectively), 6 patients averaged close to 40 mg per day (38, 40, 40, 44, 45, and 50 mg, respectively), and 3 patients averaged daily doses of 80 mg (74, 78, and 104 mg, respectively) while on study. Adiponectin and IL-18 were evaluated as markers of selective BDII inhibition and ABBV-744 activity, respectively. There was a dose-dependent increase in adiponectin (supplemental Figure 2A), suggestive of more BDII-specific inhibition with the lowest daily ABBV-744 doses (ie, ∼20 mg); these lower doses were still biologically active as demonstrated by the concomitant reduction of IL-18 (supplemental Figure 2B). Although there was evidence indicating ABBV-744 also modulates proteins associated with NF-κB signaling (eg, B2M, C-reactive protein, CD40 ligand),20 constitutional symptoms (eg, TIMP-1),21 and survival (ie, IL-8),22 a dose-dependent trend was not observed (data not shown).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: This phase 1b, open-label study represents, to our knowledge, the first investigation of ABBV-744 monotherapy in patients with MF, a population with significant unmet therapeutic needs and limited treatment options. Consistent with this class of agents, the most commonly observed TEAEs were thrombocytopenia (67%), diarrhea (62%), anemia (48%), and nausea (33%). DLTs, primarily thrombocytopenia and anemia, occurred at all dose levels and were observed in 52% of patients. With respect to efficacy, SVR35 was reached in 33% of patients at week 24, and symptom control (TSS50) in 29% of patients by week 12, outcomes and clinical improvement that are particularly noteworthy in this heavily pretreated population. ABBV-744 exposures in patients with R/R MF were generally consistent with those observed in patients with R/R AML.16

Previously, the safety profile of ABBV-744 was reported in a cohort of 30 patients with R/R AML, which informed the starting dose used in this study.16 Similar to this study, all patients experienced TEAEs, including a high proportion with grade ≥3 TEAEs (97% of the R/R AML cohort vs 86% of patients with R/R MF). Treatment discontinuation due to AEs was lower in the R/R MF cohort (14%) vs the R/R AML study population (43%),16 possibly due to the lower doses assessed in this study. GI AEs and cytopenias were still the most common TEAEs for both patient populations and treatment exposure duration in patients with R/R MF were generally consistent with those observed in patients with R/R AML.16 Two patients in the R/R AML cohort had clinical improvement, 1 with a partial remission and 1 with a morphologic leukemia-free state,16 which is consistent with the limited monotherapy efficacy response observed in this study of patients with R/R MF.

As the first BD-selective BETi to enter clinical trials, ABBV-744 is ∼300-fold more selective for the 4 BET BDII relative to corresponding BDI.23 Clinically, in MF, observed increases in adiponectin19 can be linked to BDI inhibition,24 whereas pan-BETis (ie, inhibition of both BDI and BDII) modulate IL-18.18,25 In this study, the level of adiponectin induction achieved with the highest doses of ABBV-744 was suggestive of BDI, or inhibition achieved with a pan-BETi (supplemental Figure 2A), whereas BDII-specific inhibition (ie, little adiponectin induction) was suggested with the lowest daily doses (ie, ∼20 mg). Alternatively, low levels of adiponectin induction could also result from low levels of biological activity, rather than BDII specificity. However, the substantial and similar levels of IL-18 reduction (supplemental Figure 2B) observed across all doses indicate high biological activity with the lowest ABBV-744 daily doses assessed, differentiating ABBV-744 from pan-BETi–like mivebresib and pelabresib.15

In this study, we hypothesized that selective BDII inhibition by ABBV-744 may diminish class-effect toxicities relative to pan-BETis, including pelabresib. There are data from 2 pan-BETis that have reported safety and efficacy outcomes in patients with solid tumors or R/R MF that are helpful to consider. First, mivebresib, an oral, small-molecule pan-BETi, was investigated in a phase 1 dose-escalation study in 84 heavily pretreated patients with locally advanced or metastatic solid tumors.12 TEAEs were reported in 96% of all patients, and TEAEs related to mivebresib were reported in 88% of all patients. The most common TEAEs related to mivebresib were dysgeusia (49%), thrombocytopenia (48%), fatigue (26%), and nausea (25%). Grade 3/4 TEAEs related to mivebresib were reported in 57% of all patients, and the most common grade 3/4 TEAEs were thrombocytopenia (35%) and anemia (6%). DLTs included thrombocytopenia, GI bleed, hypertension, fatigue, decreased appetite, and aspartate aminotransferase elevation. All patients with solid tumors discontinued mivebresib.12

A second pan-BETi, pelabresib, has been investigated in patients with hematological malignancies, including MF in the MANIFEST trial. An MTD was established in a phase 1 trial of 64 heavily pretreated patients (median number of previous lines of systemic therapy, 4 [range, 1-12]) with R/R lymphoma.26 RDI was considered high (between 70% and 100% across dose cycles) and IL-18 suppression was observed,27 consistent with BET inhibition. The most common hematological TEAEs were thrombocytopenia (45%) and anemia (25%); the most common nonhematological TEAEs were fatigue (36%), nausea (28%), and decreased appetite (27%). Of 64 patients, 4 (6%) had an overall response and 21 (33%) had stable disease.26 Based on these outcomes, MANIFEST, a phase 2 study investigating pelabresib for patients with MF, was initiated. In the arm-1 cohort of the MANIFEST trial, patients with advanced MF who were refractory/intolerant to, or ineligible for, JAKis received pelabresib monotherapy. Similar to the dose-finding study, of the 46 patients who were evaluable for safety, the most common hematological TEAEs were thrombocytopenia (30%) and anemia, and the most common nonhematological TEAEs were nausea (39%), diarrhea (37%), asthenic conditions (30%), dysgeusia (30%), respiratory tract infections (28%), cough (26%), constipation (22%), and weight decrease (22%).28 In addition to evaluating pelabresib monotherapy, the MANIFEST trial enrolled patients with JAKi treatment-naïve MF into the arm-3 cohort to evaluate pelabresib combined with ruxolitinib. Among 84 patients treated with pelabresib with ruxolitinib, the most common TEAEs (≥20%) included thrombocytopenia (52%), anemia (42%), diarrhea (35%), fatigue (33%), musculoskeletal pain (30%), respiratory tract infections (29%), dizziness (26%), constipation (25%), nausea (24%), abdominal pain (23%), dysgeusia (21%), and dyspnea (20%).14 TEAEs that led to discontinuation were reported in 4% of patients.14

Most recently, the randomized phase 3 MANIFEST-2 trial reported the outcomes of combination ruxolitinib and pelabresib vs ruxolitinib and placebo in patients with JAKi-naïve MF with intermediate 1 and higher disease.20 The MANIFEST-2 trial demonstrated superior spleen reduction with combination pelabresib, and nominal improvement in symptom reduction favoring combination therapy. Multiple biomarkers of disease burden suggested greater disease modification with the addition of pelabresib to ruxolitinib. Importantly, the combination was well tolerated and cytopenias and GI toxicity were the most notable, yet manageable, TEAEs.20 An imbalance in the number of cases of early disease evolution to blast phase were reported with pelabresib.20 However, the mechanism underlying this concern makes the actual relationship to pelabresib uncertain.

Overall, the safety profile of ABBV-744 was consistent with that of pan-BETis, as demonstrated by mivebresib and pelabresib, with cytopenias and GI TEAEs being the most common. Efficacy observed in the dose-finding study of pelabresib and arm 1 of the MANIFEST study was also generally similar to that of ABBV-744, with a limited number of patients achieving complete or partial remissions.

As was demonstrated by the clinical development of pelabresib, continuous dosing with adequate drug exposure is important for disease control and overall efficacy but must be balanced with tolerance. The initial phase 1 study of pelabresib established that 21-day cycles with 14 days of continuous once-daily pelabresib dosing followed by a 7-day break achieved continuous inhibition whereas also allowing for recovery from on-target tissue toxicity, including thrombocytopenia.26 Subsequent clinical studies used this same dosing approach for pelabresib but added continuous ruxolitinib twice daily because the benefits of a BETi were enhanced when combined with a JAKi.14,20 In our study, patients had a median of 2 dose interruptions with ABBV-744, regardless of continuous or intermittent dosing; however, the range of interruptions was much higher in patients in the continuous 120-mg cohort than either the continuous 80- or 40-mg cohorts. As a result, the median treatment duration generally increased as dose decreased, with a median of 25 cycles at 40 mg vs a median of 4 cycles at 120 mg, reflecting better tolerance of ABBV-744 at these doses (Table 3). Because this study focused exclusively on monotherapy, the potential of ABBV-744 in combination regimens remains to be determined. The findings indicate that ABBV-744 monotherapy may not be sufficient in this heavily pretreated patient population and may potentially require combination regimens to achieve a higher level of efficacy.

Certain limitations of this study should be noted. First, the single-arm design did not allow for direct comparison with any other therapy. Second, and perhaps most significantly, is the impact of the small sample size overall and per dose level, which affects our ability to draw meaningful conclusions from the data. Although a tolerable dose of ABBV-744 (180 mg) was identified in patients with AML,16 there may be limited applicability in translating tolerability to patients with MF. This is underscored by the significant dose reductions and discontinuations before first assessment in our study, making interpretability by dose level difficult and limiting the impact of efficacy. In addition to reductions and discontinuations occurring before first efficacy assessment, the high number of patients requiring dose interruptions (71%) may have affected efficacy and robust assessment of tolerability.

BETis continue to have promise in the treatment of solid and hematological malignancies but progress has been challenging. In this trial of ABBV-744 in MF, evaluation of the hypothesis that selective targeting of BDII with ABBV-744 could substantially improve safety over pan-BETis was likely confounded, because safety and efficacy outcomes at higher doses were suggestive of pan-BETis rather than BDII domain-selective BETis. In addition, the limited number of patients at the most selective doses makes it difficult to differentiate outcomes from those of pan-BETis such as pelabresib. To fully test the hypothesis, additional approaches are needed. Given the limited clinical activity with monotherapy administration and a toxicity profile that requires further characterization before combination with other agents, the remaining segments of the original study design were not enrolled and the development of ABBV-744 in MF was discontinued.
